prompt: The bookshop's tests run on JUnit 6.0.3, and most articles say "JUnit 5". What is the relation between the two?

choices.text: JUnit 6 is JUnit 4 under a new name, and the Jupiter API was dropped
choices.why: No. JUnit 4 is the older API, `org.junit.Test`. The tests here import `org.junit.jupiter.api`, which is Jupiter, and Jupiter is what JUnit 6 kept.

choices.text: JUnit 6 continues JUnit 5's Jupiter model: same packages, same annotations
choices.why: Right. JUnit 6 kept the annotations of `org.junit.jupiter.api`, raised the minimum Java to 17 and put all its parts on one version number.

choices.text: JUnit 5 and JUnit 6 are two engines that Spring Boot runs side by side on every build
choices.why: No. The dependency tree shows one `junit-jupiter`, at 6.0.3. There is no separate JUnit 5 engine in the project.

choices.text: JUnit 6 moved the annotations to a new package, so every JUnit 5 test needs its imports rewritten
choices.why: No. The imports in `IsbnTest` are `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test` and friends, the same packages JUnit 5 introduced in 2017.

prompt: Match each piece to what it does when you type `mvn test` in the bookshop.

pairs.right: finds the test classes by name and runs them in a JVM of its own
discovers the tests and hands each one to an engine
brings JUnit, AssertJ and Mockito in the test scope

prompt: Before this lesson, `mvn test` on the bookshop printed `No tests to run.` and then `BUILD SUCCESS`. What does that pair tell you?
hint: Read the verdict and the line just before it separately.

choices.text: That surefire was missing from the pom and Maven skipped the phase
choices.why: No. The line above it names `maven-surefire-plugin:3.5.6:test`: surefire ran, and found nothing to run.

choices.text: That every test of the project passed
choices.why: There were none. A success with no tests is not a statement about any code.

choices.text: That a run with no tests counts as a success in Maven
choices.why: Right. Nothing fails when nothing runs, which is why the misnamed class later in the lesson passes the build too.

choices.text: That the JUnit engine refused the project because the starter was not there yet
choices.why: No engine was involved. Without the starter, surefire had no JUnit Platform to hand anything to, and no test classes either.

prompt: `IsbnTest` and its methods are declared without `public`. Why does that work?

choices.text: Jupiter reaches them by reflection, whatever their visibility
choices.why: Right. JUnit 4 required `public`; Jupiter does not, so the tests can stay package-private.

choices.text: Because Maven makes every class in src/test/java public when it compiles them
choices.why: Maven compiles the sources as written. Visibility is the Java source's, and the test class stays package-private.

choices.text: Because a test class in the same package as `Isbn` inherits its visibility
choices.why: Classes do not inherit visibility from their neighbours. Sharing the package only lets the test see package-private members of `Isbn`.

choices.text: It works only when the tests are run from an IDE, not from Maven
choices.why: The lesson ran them from Maven: `Tests run: 3`. Surefire hands them to the same Platform an IDE uses.

prompt: A test calls a method that throws `NullPointerException` before the test reaches its assertion. How does surefire report that test?

choices.text: Under Failures, because the test did not pass
choices.why: Failures are assertions that did not hold. This test never reached its assertion.

choices.text: Under Skipped, because the assertion never ran
choices.why: Skipped is for a test that was deliberately not run. This one ran and threw.

choices.text: As passed, because no assertion failed
choices.why: A test passes only if nothing it calls throws. An exception escaping the test is never a pass.

choices.text: Under Errors, and the build fails
choices.why: Right. An error is any exception other than a failed assertion; it fails the build, and it says the code never got as far as answering.

prompt: Surefire runs a class only when its name matches an include pattern. Renamed `IsbnChecks`, the class compiled and nothing ran; renamed back to `Isbn___`, its three methods ran again.
hint: The default patterns are four, and the bookshop's class names use one of them.

prompt: Which statements about the commands this section ran are true? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: `mvn -q test` printed nothing when every test passed
choices.why: Right. `-q` keeps warnings and errors only, so a passing run leaves just the exit code.

choices.text: `-Dtest='IsbnTest#refusesNull'` ran a single test
choices.why: Right. `Tests run: 1`: the class, then one method after `#`.

choices.text: `-q` skips the tests to make the build quicker
choices.why: That is `-DskipTests`. `-q` only changes how much Maven prints; the tests ran and the exit code was 0.

choices.text: After this lesson, a failing test also stops `mvn package` from building the jar
choices.why: Right. `package` comes after `test` in the lifecycle, so the tests run first and a failure stops the build.

choices.text: `-q` hides failing tests, so a broken build exits with 0
choices.why: `-q` hides information messages, not errors: a failure is still printed and the exit code is still non-zero.

prompt: A test class has one method with `@ParameterizedTest` and `@ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3})`, one with `@ParameterizedTest` and a `@CsvSource` of four rows, and two plain `@Test` methods. What number does surefire print after `Tests run:` for this class?
`refusesAnythingElse` carries `@ParameterizedTest(name = "{1}: {0}")` and takes `(String isbn, String reason)`. What does the pattern do?

choices.text: It tells `@CsvSource` to read the second column before the first
choices.why: The columns go to the parameters in order whatever the pattern says: `isbn` is still the first column.

choices.text: It renames the test method in surefire's XML report
choices.why: The XML still says `refusesAnythingElse(String, String)[1]`. The pattern names the display name, not the method.

choices.text: It names each invocation by the reason, then the ISBN
choices.why: Right. `{1}` is the second argument and `{0}` the first, so the launcher printed `"a hyphen": "978-6500000016"`.

choices.text: It makes the assertion print the reason when the test fails
choices.why: The assertion is `assertFalse`, and its message is the same whatever the name; `reason` is never passed to it.

prompt: A colleague says the `name` pattern on a parameterised test is useless, because `mvn test` never prints it. Which reply is accurate?

choices.text: Surefire does print it, as the test's name in the `Tests run` line
choices.why: The `Tests run` line names the class, and the failure line names `acceptsAValidIsbn13(String)[3]`. The pattern was not in either.

choices.text: It is right about surefire, and the names are for whatever shows JUnit's display names: an IDE's test window, or the console launcher
choices.why: Right. Surefire reports by signature and index; the launcher and the IDEs show the names JUnit builds from the pattern.

choices.text: The pattern also decides the order the invocations run in, so it is not useless
choices.why: The invocations run in the order of the source's rows; the pattern only names them.

choices.text: It is right, and the pattern only has an effect under JUnit 4
choices.why: JUnit 4 had no `@ParameterizedTest`. The pattern is Jupiter's, and the launcher printed the names it builds.

prompt: Put these lines of the failing run in the order surefire printed them, top to bottom.
hint: The class line, then the detail, then the totals, then the verdict.
items: Tests run: 10, Failures: 1 ... <<< FAILURE! -- in com.example.bookshop.catalogue.IsbnTest

prompt: With the outer `% 10` removed, taking Frankenstein's `9786500000030` out of `@ValueSource` turned the run green. Why could none of the three remaining ISBNs catch the bug?

choices.text: Because the three remaining ISBNs are tested by `refusesAnythingElse`, which expects `false`
choices.why: They are in `acceptsAValidIsbn13`, which expects `true`, and they still got `true` from the broken rule.

choices.text: Because surefire stops comparing after the first ISBN that passes
choices.why: Every invocation runs and reports on its own: the run said `Tests run: 9`.

choices.text: Because their check digits are not 0, and the outer `% 10` only changes the result when the sum already ends in 0
choices.why: Right. For any other sum, `10 - sum % 10` is already below 10 and the outer `% 10` leaves it alone, so both rules agree on those three.

choices.text: Because `9780306406157` has a different prefix, so the rule treats it separately
choices.why: The rule never looks at the prefix: it weighs all twelve digits the same way for every ISBN.

prompt: Keep the broken rule, `int check = 10 - sum % 10;`. How many of these five valid ISBNs does `Isbn.isValid` still accept: `9786500000016`, `9786500000023`, `9786500000030`, `9780306406157`, `9786500000160`?
hint: Look only at the last digit of each.

prompt: The failure said only `expected: <true> but was: <false>`. Why did it not name the ISBN that failed?

choices.text: Because surefire shortens every assertion message to its first few words
choices.why: Surefire printed AssertJ's messages over several lines later in the lesson. It prints what the assertion gives it.

choices.text: Because `assertTrue` receives only a boolean and has nothing else to report
choices.why: Right. The ISBN was gone by the time `assertTrue` was called; the index `[3]` in the test's name is what pointed at it.

choices.text: Because JUnit hides test arguments from the output unless a flag enables them
choices.why: No flag is involved. The launcher showed the arguments in the names without being asked; the assertion never had them.

choices.text: Because the message is inverted: the rule returned true and the test expected false
choices.why: The test is `acceptsAValidIsbn13`, which expects `true`; the broken rule returned `false` for Frankenstein.

prompt: JUnit runs the three tests of `BookTest.Take`. How many instances of `BookTest` does it create?

choices.text: One, shared by the three tests
choices.why: That is TestNG's model. Jupiter's default is a new instance per test method.

choices.text: Three, one for each test
choices.why: Right. Each test gets a new `BookTest` and a new `Take` inside it, and `@BeforeEach` runs on each.

choices.text: None, because the tests are in the nested class
choices.why: `Take` is an inner class, and an inner instance cannot exist without an outer one.

choices.text: Six, two for each test
choices.why: Two objects per test, yes, but only one of them is a `BookTest`; the other is a `Take`.

prompt: With `@BeforeAll` and a `static` book, two of the three `take` tests failed. What was wrong?

choices.text: `take` itself, which only fails when the book is static
choices.why: `Book.take` was unchanged and passed under `@BeforeEach`. The tests shared one book, which is a property of the test, not of the code.

choices.text: `@BeforeAll` ran after the tests instead of before them
choices.why: It ran once, before all of them, which is the problem: one book for three tests that each change it.

choices.text: The two failing tests, whose expectations were written for a different book
choices.why: Their expectations are right for a book with two copies. They received a book somebody else had already emptied.

choices.text: The fixture: one shared book, emptied by `lowersTheStock` first
choices.why: Right. `but was: <0>` and `Only 0 of 'Dom Casmurro' left` are both the trace of the first test's `take(2)`.

prompt: Which statements about AssertJ, as `OrderTest` uses it, are true? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: `assertThat` starts from the actual value, and the method after it states what is expected
choices.why: Right. `assertThat(order.totalCents()).isEqualTo(11670)` reads actual, then expected.

choices.text: `containsExactly(2, 1)` fails if the quantities are right but in another order
choices.why: Right. The detour with `(1, 2)` failed on both positions.

choices.text: Its failure message showed both lists and each index where they differed
choices.why: Right. That is the reason the lesson gives for preferring it on collections.

choices.text: Using AssertJ means JUnit's engine is no longer needed to run the test
choices.why: AssertJ is only assertions. `OrderTest` still has `@Test`, and the Jupiter engine still runs it.

choices.text: `isEqualTo` compares two `int` values with `==` on their references
choices.why: An `int` has no reference. `isEqualTo` compares values, and the message showed `expected: 11680` and `but was: 11670`.

prompt: A run of the whole project prints `Tests run: 3 ... -- in take` and then `Tests run: 0 ... -- in com.example.bookshop.catalogue.BookTest`. What happened to `BookTest`?

choices.text: They ran in the nested class, which surefire reports as `take`
choices.why: Right. The outer class has no test methods of its own, so it reports zero; the total at the bottom still counts 15.

choices.text: Its tests were discovered but skipped, because `@DisplayName` disables a class
choices.why: A skipped test is counted under `Skipped`, which says 0. `@DisplayName` only names.

choices.text: Its tests ran twice, once as `take` and once as `BookTest`
choices.why: The total is 15, which is 2 + 3 + 10: each test of `take` counted once.

choices.text: Its name does not end in `Test`, so surefire ignored it
choices.why: `BookTest` ends in `Test`, and surefire did run it: `Running com.example.bookshop.catalogue.BookTest`.

prompt: In `BookTest`, the method that builds a new book with two copies before every test is annotated `@___`.
`ShelfTest` calls `assertEquals(shelf.count("Dom Casmurro"), 2)` from `org.testng.Assert`. Which argument is which?

choices.text: The first is expected and the second actual, as in JUnit
choices.why: That is JUnit's order. TestNG's is the reverse, which is why a line copied between them blames the wrong side.

choices.text: The order does not matter, because the two values are only compared
choices.why: The comparison does not care; the message does. The run said `expected [3] but found [2]` because the arguments were in TestNG's order.

choices.text: The first is actual and the second expected
choices.why: Right. TestNG puts the actual value first, the reverse of JUnit's `assertEquals`.

choices.text: The first is the message to print and the second the value to check
choices.why: The message is an optional third argument in TestNG; both of these are values.

prompt: `takesOne` has `dependsOnMethods = "addsCopies"`. When `addsCopies` failed, what did TestNG do with `takesOne`?

choices.text: Ran it on a fresh `Shelf`, so it failed with an exception
choices.why: TestNG keeps one instance per class, and it did not run `takesOne` at all: `Skipped: 1`.

choices.text: Skipped it, and the result file marked it `SKIP`
choices.why: Right. A test whose dependency failed is not run, so the report has one failure instead of two.

choices.text: Ran it anyway and counted it as a second failure
choices.why: The summary said `Failures: 1`; the second test was `SKIP`, not `FAIL`.

choices.text: Ran it first, because a dependency reverses the order
choices.why: A dependency puts the depended-on method first; `takesOne` waits for `addsCopies`.

prompt: Why does a Spring Boot project like the bookshop use JUnit rather than TestNG?

choices.text: Because TestNG cannot run on Java 25
choices.why: `~/testng-look` built and ran six tests on the same JDK 25.

choices.text: Because Spring has no support for TestNG at all
choices.why: Spring supports it through `AbstractTestNGSpringContextTests`; it is the less travelled road, not a closed one.

choices.text: Because JUnit has features TestNG lacks, such as data providers and groups
choices.why: Those are TestNG's features; Jupiter has its own versions of them. The choice is not about features.

choices.text: Because the starter brings Jupiter, and Boot's test annotations are Jupiter extensions that a TestNG class does not read
choices.why: Right. `@SpringBootTest` carries `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)`, which only Jupiter reads.

prompt: Match each TestNG feature from `~/testng-look` to what a JUnit Jupiter project uses for the same job.

pairs.right: nothing: Jupiter's tests are meant to be independent

prompt: A teammate adds `src/test/java/com/example/bookshop/ordering/PriceRules.java` with five `@Test` methods. For weeks `mvn package` is green, and then a pricing bug those tests would have caught reaches production. What is the most likely reason?
hint: Compare the class name with the four patterns surefire uses by default.

choices.text: The `test` scope keeps classes in src/test/java out of the build
choices.why: The scope is about dependencies. Classes in src/test/java are compiled, and the build compiled `IsbnChecks` the same way.

choices.text: Surefire never ran it: the name matches no include pattern
choices.why: Right. The class compiles and nothing runs it, and a run with nothing in it is a success.

choices.text: `mvn package` does not run tests unless `-Dtest` names them
choices.why: `package` comes after `test` in the lifecycle, and runs every class surefire's patterns select.

choices.text: The tests passed because AssertJ was missing from the classpath
choices.why: A missing library fails compilation, which would have turned the build red.

prompt: `ShelfTest` is ported to JUnit Jupiter: `org.testng` imports become Jupiter's, the `dependsOnMethods` attributes are dropped, and the field `private final Shelf shelf = new Shelf();` stays. Whatever order JUnit picks, what happens to `takesOne`?

choices.text: It passes if JUnit happens to run `addsCopies` first, and fails otherwise
choices.why: Order would matter if the instance were shared. In Jupiter `takesOne` has its own `ShelfTest`, so `addsCopies` never touches its shelf.

choices.text: It is skipped, because JUnit sees that it needs `addsCopies`
choices.why: Nothing tells JUnit that any more; the attribute was dropped, and Jupiter has no such skip.

choices.text: It passes, because the field is initialised once for the whole class
choices.why: That is TestNG's model. Jupiter builds a new instance, and so a new empty `Shelf`, for every test.

choices.text: Errors: its own empty shelf makes `take` throw `IllegalStateException`
choices.why: Right. A fresh instance means a fresh empty shelf, and an exception other than a failed assertion is an error.
